ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: The figure shows a pedigree. The top individual #1 is a circle, and mates with square individual #2; their offspring include square #3 and circle #4. #3 and an outside circle mate on the left give birth to circle #5; #4 and an outside square mate on the right give birth to square #6. #5 and #6 are connected by a double line, indicating consanguineous mating, and their offspring is bottom circle #7. Reasoning: This disease is a rare autosomal recessive disease. It is known that #1 is a heterozygous carrier and #2 is not a carrier, so each of their children #3 and #4 each has a 1/2 probability of becoming a carrier. The question also states that the spouses of #3 and #4 are both not carriers, therefore the probability that #5 becomes a carrier is P(#3 carries)×P(#3 transmits the disease-causing allele)=1/2×1/2=1/4; similarly, the probability that #6 becomes a carrier is also 1/2×1/2=1/4. For #7 to have an autosomal recessive disease, #5 and #6 must both be carriers, and both people must transmit the disease-causing allele to #7; if both people are carriers, the probability that the offspring is affected is 1/4. Therefore the total probability is (1/4)×(1/4)×(1/4)=1/64.

raw_record.question_text: If individual #1 in the following pedigree shown in the figure is a heterozygote for a rare, AR disease, what is the probability that individual #7 will be affected by the disease? Assume that #2 and the spouses of #3 and #4 are not carriers.

method.method_draft: First describe the pedigree from the image, then compute carrier risks down the two branches. Since #1 is a heterozygote and #2 is not a carrier, each of their children #3 and #4 has probability 1/2 of being a carrier. The outside spouses of #3 and #4 are noncarriers, so #5 has carrier probability (1/2)(1/2)=1/4 and #6 also has carrier probability (1/2)(1/2)=1/4. Individual #7 is affected only if both #5 and #6 are carriers and both transmit the recessive allele, so multiply (1/4)(1/4)(1/4)=1/64.
